Thanks for sharing. Appreciate the thoughts on framing and interpretation of the film as I just watched it last night. Definitely a compelling and fun watch but I’m still wrapping my head around what I like and possibly dislike. I didn’t feel like there was a “twist” so much as the end (Oliver’s manipulative and eventual murderous manner) felt telegraphed pretty early on to me. By the time Oliver spoke with the Mum about Pamela’s stories being inconsistent (after she was expelled) I thought, “Oh yeah, Oliver is killing Felix.” 

Regarding Oliver’s infatuation with Felix, I wasn’t thinking Call Me By Your Name as much as The Talented Mr. Ripley vibes throughout. I’m not sure where I started to feel that precisely but it was before the film moved to Saltburn for the setting. The movie seemed to be trying to establish him as a sympathetic lower class character amidst a contemptuous rich elite but I didn’t trust him as a character from very early on.

Just thinking more about this: do you think the film would be stronger/better if Oliver’s manipulations were confirmed throughout the film and not saved for the end? 

Ultimately, I think the film was unsuccessfully going for a wolf-in-sheep’s clothing by withholding those moments (piercing the bike tire, poisoning Felix, etc) for a reveal at the end but am now wondering if the power dynamic of the film would be more intriguing, better executed if we were shown Oliver’s manipulations as they occurred. 

To be clear too, I really enjoyed the film overall and I wasn’t too bothered by the “twist” but just felt it was underwhelmingly obvious.

As a gay man, Saltburn is among the straightest films that thinks it's gay I've ever seen. I do not think its truly about seductive desire or queer obsession. It chickens out of all of that stuff. Its provocative moments aren't actually particularly provocative aside from eliciting a disgust reaction, and the queerness is essentially entirely implied between the two leads. As you've said OP the 3rd act shits the bed as well. 

TLDR I think any comparison to Call me By Your Name is absurd and smacks of "getting boss baby vibes from this" level film analysis

While I get yours and other peoples points about the movie, in my opinion the gay school boy love story is just a Trojan horse for the social climber narrative which is what I think Fennel was getting to. And because she does the first act so well it is easy to get disappointed by the ending but at least when I watched the movie I felt uneasy since the beginning so I don’t think it is really a twist but more of a reveal. There were always little things about Oliver that rang very untrue so I don’t think we as an audience are meant to trust him at face value… the issue is the other side of characters is so easily dislikable that you hold to him as your sense of normality (who wouldn’t fancy Felix really) 

It’s interesting seeing how many people disliked this movie

I think the "twist" at the end makes Oliver's intentions concrete for the viewer. When I watched the scene where Oliver talks about Pamela with Felix's mum, I saw it as Oliver's attempt to grow closer with the family through gossip. "Gossip is actually one of the societal forces that brings us together and helps maintain social order." For a moment, Oliver can feel part of a higher social class. But maybe it is just my optimistic view which is giving me tunnel vision. In hindsight, I agree that it is a sign of Oliver's takeover.

I commented on another post about how I expected it to be CMBYN 2.0 because my Twitter timeline was talking about the Jacob Elordi cum eating interview a lot and the movie ended up making me feel *nothing.* No tension whatsoever. I kept forgetting Felix even existed because Oliver had more tension with the butler than him.

Why would anyone think this film is gay or about gay love? The character is a vampire, as such sex and seduction are tools the character uses in order to gain what he actually wants: status. The film has a lot more in common with Woody Allen's film Match Point. Like Rhys Meyers' character in Match Point, Oliver Quick is a social climber. The difference is that Rhys Myers' character wants Scarlett Johannson, while Quick wants Saltburn (and the lifestyle/status it brings). The sexual aspects of Quick are only ever used to gain favor, not as a release in and of itself. I don't think we actually ever seen Quick having sex (or killing). He gets off by absorbing the essence(s) of the privileged classes (like a vampire or a parasite).

Felix was a means to an end. The moment Felix's knowledge about Oliver's true past threatened his foothold on Saltburn, Felix mysteriously died (or was removed). It was always about Saltburn, and the lifestyle and privilege it represents.
15 minutes could easily have been shaved off and it would've made for a more satisfying film.
